items.stem: What is the appearance of bromine at room temperature?
items.answer: a red-brown liquid

items.stem: Explain why the boiling points of the halogens increase down the group.
items.answer: Molecules have more electrons, so stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces; more energy is needed to separate them.
items.markingKey: more electrons [1]; stronger London forces [1]

items.stem: Explain why the thermal stability of the hydrogen halides decreases from HF to HI.
items.answer: The halogen atom becomes larger so the H–X bond is longer and weaker; less energy is needed to break it.
items.markingKey: longer bond [1]; weaker, less energy to break [1]

items.stem: A red-hot wire is plunged into separate tubes of HCl, HBr and HI. Predict and explain what is seen in the tube of HBr. Use the bond energies H–Cl 431, H–Br 366, H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.answer: Slight orange-brown colour: some HBr decomposes to Br₂.
items.markingKey: correct observation [1]; linked to bond energy [1]

items.stem: A red-hot wire is plunged into separate tubes of HCl, HBr and HI. Predict and explain what is seen in the tube of HI. Use the bond energies H–Cl 431, H–Br 366, H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹. Write an equation for any decomposition.
items.answer: Purple vapour: HI decomposes into H₂ and I₂ because the H–I bond is weakest. 2HI → H₂ + I₂
items.markingKey: correct observation [1]; linked to bond energy [1]; equation 2HX → H₂ + X₂ where relevant [1]

items.stem: Zara is preparing a poster on the physical properties of the Group 17 elements for a school in Madrid. (a) Explain the trend in volatility. (b) Draw a dot-and-cross diagram of HCl and state the type of intermolecular force.
items.answer: (a) Decreases: more electrons, stronger London forces. (b) Shared pair H–Cl with three lone pairs on Cl; pd-pd (plus London) forces.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the colour of iodine vapour? (b) Why is the F–F bond weaker than the Cl–Cl bond?

items.markingKey: (a) Iodine sublimes on warming to a purple vapour. (b) Short bond brings non-bonding pairs close together.

items.stem: Explain why HCl is a gas but HF is a liquid on a cold day (bp 20 °C).

items.stem: Which halogen is the strongest oxidising agent?
items.answer: fluorine

items.stem: Explain why chlorine displaces bromine from aqueous potassium bromide but iodine does not.
items.answer: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine (its atom more readily gains an electron, smaller with less shielding); iodine is weaker than bromine.
items.markingKey: oxidising power Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ [1]; reason in terms of electron gain [1]

items.stem: Explain why bromide ions can reduce concentrated sulfuric acid but chloride ions cannot.
items.answer: Br⁻ is larger, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost; Br⁻ is a stronger reducing agent than Cl⁻.
items.markingKey: Br⁻ larger, loses electron more easily [1]; stronger reducing agent [1]

items.stem: Mei adds aqueous iodine to aqueous sodium bromide, then shakes the mixture with cyclohexane. Describe what is seen and write an ionic equation for any reaction.

items.stem: Kenji adds aqueous chlorine to aqueous potassium iodide, then shakes the mixture with cyclohexane. Describe what is seen and write an ionic equation for any reaction. Explain your answer in terms of the relative oxidising power of the halogens.
items.answer: Aqueous layer turns brown; cyclohexane layer violet/purple. Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂ Oxidising power decreases down the group (Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂): the halogen atom is larger and attracts an extra electron less strongly, so chlorine can oxidise iodide ions.

Identify the anion in Q and explain how each result supports your answer.
items.answer: chloride (Cl⁻): white precipitate is characteristic of chloride; precipitate dissolves in dilute ammonia is characteristic of chloride
items.markingKey: chloride identified [1]; result interpreted [1] result interpreted [1]

items.stem: Freya adds aqueous chlorine to aqueous sodium bromide, then shakes the mixture with cyclohexane. Describe what is seen and write an ionic equation for any reaction.
items.answer: Aqueous layer turns orange/yellow; cyclohexane layer orange-red. Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂
items.markingKey: reaction or no reaction correctly predicted [1]; colours [1]; ionic equation [1]

items.stem: A forensic laboratory in Cape Town analyses an unknown sodium halide, which is sodium iodide. (a) Write an equation for the redox reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid, if any. (b) Explain the trend in reducing power of the halide ions. (c) Write an ionic equation for the reaction of chlorine water with this halide, if any.
items.answer: (a) 8HI + H₂SO₄ → 4I₂ + H₂S + 4H₂O (b) Increases Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻: larger ions, outer electrons further from nucleus and more shielded, more easily lost. (c) Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂
items.markingKey: (a) 8HI + H₂SO₄ → 4I₂ + H₂S + 4H₂O [1] (b) Increases Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻: larger ions, outer electrons further from nucleus and more shielded, more easily lost. [2] (c) Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂ [1]

items.stem: A forensic laboratory in Doha analyses an unknown sodium halide, which is sodium chloride. (a) Describe the silver nitrate test and the results for each halide. (b) State the observations with concentrated sulfuric acid for sodium chloride.
items.answer: (a) Acidify with HNO₃, add AgNO₃(aq): Cl⁻ white, Br⁻ cream, I⁻ yellow; confirm with NH₃(aq). (b) steamy white fumes of HCl
items.markingKey: (a) Acidify with HNO₃, add AgNO₃(aq): Cl⁻ white, Br⁻ cream, I⁻ yellow; confirm with NH₃(aq). [3] (b) steamy white fumes of HCl [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the oxidation number of chlorine in NaClO₃? (b) What forms when chlorine reacts with cold dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide?
items.answer: (a) +5 (b) sodium chloride, sodium chlorate(I) and water
items.markingKey: (a) Na +1, O −2 ×3: Cl = +5. (b) Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.

items.stem: Leila investigates the reactions of chlorine with sodium hydroxide in a school laboratory. Explain why the products of chlorine with NaOH depend on temperature.
items.answer: At higher temperature chlorate(I) itself disproportionates into chloride and chlorate(V), so hot NaOH gives NaClO₃.
items.markingKey: ClO⁻ disproportionates when hot; forms ClO₃⁻ and Cl⁻ [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the reaction of chlorine with cold NaOH is a disproportionation reaction. (b) Explain why the products of chlorine with NaOH depend on temperature.
items.answer: (a) Chlorine (0) is both reduced to −1 in NaCl and oxidised to +1 in NaClO. (b) At higher temperature chlorate(I) itself disproportionates into chloride and chlorate(V), so hot NaOH gives NaClO₃.
items.markingKey: (a) 0 → −1 [1]; 0 → +1 [1] (b) ClO⁻ disproportionates when hot [1]; forms ClO₃⁻ and Cl⁻ [1]

items.stem: Use oxidation numbers to decide whether the reaction 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O is a disproportionation. Explain your answer.
items.answer: Yes: chlorine oxidation numbers 0 → −1 and +5.
items.markingKey: oxidation numbers of chlorine in all species [1]; conclusion with reason (same element both oxidised and reduced or not) [1]

items.stem: A town in Kathmandu disinfects its water supply with chlorine. (a) Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with cold dilute NaOH. (b) Define disproportionation using one of these reactions.
items.answer: (a) Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O (b) Same element simultaneously oxidised and reduced, e.g. Cl 0 → −1 and +1.
items.markingKey: (a) Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O [1] (b) Same element simultaneously oxidised and reduced, e.g. Cl 0 → −1 and +1. [2]

items.stem: Ana makes bleach in a school laboratory by passing chlorine into cold sodium hydroxide, and compares it with the product from hot sodium hydroxide. (a) Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with cold dilute NaOH. (b) Write the equation for the reaction with hot concentrated NaOH and give the oxidation numbers of chlorine in each product. (c) Define disproportionation using one of these reactions.
items.answer: (a) Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O (b) 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O; −1 and +5 (c) Same element simultaneously oxidised and reduced, e.g. Cl 0 → −1 and +1.
items.markingKey: (a) Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O [1] (b) 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O; −1 and +5 [3] (c) Same element simultaneously oxidised and reduced, e.g. Cl 0 → −1 and +1. [2]

items.stem: Why is the F–F bond weaker than the Cl–Cl bond?
options: repulsion between lone pairs on the small, close F atoms
items.answer: repulsion between lone pairs on the small, close F atoms
items.markingKey: Short bond brings non-bonding pairs close together.

items.stem: A student in Muscat explains the thermal stability of the hydrogen halides. Explain why HCl is a gas but HF is a liquid on a cold day (bp 20 °C).
items.answer: HF forms hydrogen bonds between molecules; HCl has only permanent dipole and London forces.
items.markingKey: HF hydrogen bonding; stronger than forces in HCl [2]

items.stem: A student in Colombo explains the thermal stability of the hydrogen halides. Explain why HCl is a gas but HF is a liquid on a cold day (bp 20 °C).

items.stem: Mohammed is preparing a poster on the physical properties of the Group 17 elements for a school in Muscat. Explain the trend in volatility.
items.answer: Decreases: more electrons, stronger London forces.
items.markingKey: Decreases: more electrons, stronger London forces. [2]

items.stem: Jonas is preparing a poster on the physical properties of the Group 17 elements for a school in Auckland. (a) Describe the appearance of chlorine, bromine and iodine at room temperature. (b) Explain why the F–F bond is weaker than expected.
items.answer: (a) Cl₂ pale yellow-green gas; Br₂ red-brown liquid; I₂ grey-black solid. (b) Small atoms; repulsion between lone pairs on adjacent F atoms.
items.markingKey: (a) Cl₂ pale yellow-green gas; Br₂ red-brown liquid; I₂ grey-black solid. [2] (b) Small atoms; repulsion between lone pairs on adjacent F atoms. [1]

items.stem: Kenji is preparing a poster on the physical properties of the Group 17 elements for a school in Dhaka. (a) Explain the trend in volatility. (b) Explain why the F–F bond is weaker than expected. (c) Predict the state and colour of astatine.
items.answer: (a) Decreases: more electrons, stronger London forces. (b) Small atoms; repulsion between lone pairs on adjacent F atoms. (c) Black solid (less volatile than iodine).
items.markingKey: (a) Decreases: more electrons, stronger London forces. [2] (b) Small atoms; repulsion between lone pairs on adjacent F atoms. [1] (c) Black solid (less volatile than iodine). [1]

items.stem: Which gas with a smell of bad eggs is produced when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium iodide?
items.answer: hydrogen sulfide
items.markingKey: I⁻ reduces S from +6 to −2.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a few cm³ of cyclohexane is added in halogen displacement experiments. (b) Explain why bromide ions can reduce concentrated sulfuric acid but chloride ions cannot.
items.answer: (a) Halogens are more soluble in the non-polar solvent and show distinctive colours (Br₂ orange-red, I₂ violet), making identification easier. (b) Br⁻ is larger, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost; Br⁻ is a stronger reducing agent than Cl⁻.
items.markingKey: (a) halogen dissolves in organic layer [1]; distinctive colours [1] (b) Br⁻ larger, loses electron more easily [1]; stronger reducing agent [1]

items.stem: Sipho writes in a revision note: "Iodine displaces chlorine from aqueous sodium chloride." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine, so there is no reaction.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Aisha tests a solution of an unknown calcium halide, Q. Results: concentrated sulfuric acid added to the solid: steamy fumes, purple vapour/black solid (I₂), yellow solid (S) and smell of bad eggs (H₂S); acidified aqueous silver nitrate: yellow precipitate. Identify the anion in Q and explain how each result supports your answer.
items.answer: iodide (I⁻): steamy fumes, purple vapour/black solid (I₂), yellow solid (S) and smell of bad eggs (H₂S) is characteristic of iodide; yellow precipitate is characteristic of iodide
items.markingKey: iodide identified [1]; result interpreted [1] result interpreted [1]

items.stem: Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium chloride. Describe what is seen, write an equation and explain why no further redox reaction occurs.
items.answer: Steamy white fumes of HCl; NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl; no further reaction: HCl is not a strong enough reducing agent to reduce H₂SO₄
items.markingKey: observations [1]; equation [1]; explanation in terms of reducing power of halide [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Discuss the benefits and risks of adding chlorine to drinking water. (b) Explain why the products of chlorine with NaOH depend on temperature.
items.answer: (a) Benefit: kills bacteria, preventing diseases such as cholera; risks: chlorine is toxic in high concentrations and can react with organic matter to form harmful chlorinated compounds. (b) At higher temperature chlorate(I) itself disproportionates into chloride and chlorate(V), so hot NaOH gives NaClO₃.

items.stem: "Hot NaOH and chlorine produce sodium chlorate(I)." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Hot concentrated NaOH gives sodium chlorate(V), NaClO₃, and sodium chloride.
